item.title: The Paradox of Cognitive Distortions in Clinical Training
item.description:
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

The Paradox of Cognitive Distortions in Clinical Training

When the training meant to fix distorted thinking teaches it instead.

Posted July 29, 2026

Cognitive behavioral therapy rests on a simple insight: The way we think shapes how we feel and act. When thinking becomes distorted (when we see the world in black and white, assume the worst about others’ intentions or motivations), suffering follows. Decades of clinical research have established this across anxiety, depression, and personality disorders.

What happens when required trainings for therapists encourage those same distortions?

In a recent article in Open Inquiry in Mental Health, psychologist Andrew Hartz identifies six psychological dynamics commonly embedded in diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) programs that map onto the cognitive distortions clinicians spend years helping clients overcome. As Hartz clarifies, although the term “DEI” has fallen out of favor in many institutions, the underlying ideas have not disappeared; they continue to appear in clinical training programs and mental health workplaces, sometimes repackaged under different labels. He is also careful to note that not every training that falls under this umbrella exhibits all of the dynamics he describes, but it is also far from rare for some of them to show up. These programs are not just for corporate employees; they are increasingly standard in clinical training programs, professional development requirements, and mental health institutions. Many therapists who are supposed to treat cognitive distortions are trained in environments that promote them.

Take, for example, all-or-nothing thinking. Practitioners of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) are familiar with this cognitive distortion: Clients who suffer from it believe they’re either a total success or a complete failure, with nothing in between. Hartz argues that many DEI trainings reproduce this exact structure at the group level, framing entire demographic groups as either “having power” or not, as either perpetual victims or perpetual victimizers. The nuance that power varies by context, individual, and situation is ignored, lost, flattened into buckets of all good or all bad. Because clinicians are trained according to this framework, they risk importing the same distorted lens into their therapy sessions.

Then there’s “safetyism” (a term coined by Pamela Paresky). It involves reframing minor interpersonal slights as traumatic events via trigger warnings and the like. When these practices are embedded in clinical training programs, therapists learn to treat emotional discomfort as something to avoid rather than work through. Yet CBT approaches refer to this practice as accommodation, the well-meaning instinct to remove all sources of discomfort (which, ironically, makes anxiety worse). Indeed, recent research on trigger warnings supports this concern: trigger warnings do not reduce distress in people with trauma histories, and even reinforce their beliefs that trauma is central to their identity.

Finally, Hartz argues that many DEI frameworks present individual outcomes as almost entirely determined by systemic forces (think “structural racism,” “the patriarchy”), potentially undermining the very sense of agency that good therapists ought to cultivate in their clients. On this point, too, the research is consistent: People who believe external forces determine their outcomes tend to experience more depression, anxiety, and helplessness than those who maintain a sense of personal agency, and these externality trends have been rising for decades.

None of this means that inclusion, fairness, and respect for diversity are bad goals; the issue is that certain elements of these trainings actively encourage the very distortions effective therapy should be trying to reduce.

Hartz concludes that if diversity training is to be part of clinical education, it should look very different, emphasizing shared humanity, encouraging dialogue across viewpoints, fostering resilience, and discussing diversity within demographic groups, not just between them.

The irony of all this is hard to miss: The mental health field, which built its modern evidence base on identifying and correcting cognitive distortions, has allowed programs promoting those very distortions to flourish within its own training institutions. “Do as I say, not as I do” is not a credible clinical philosophy. Therapists who are trained to think in distorted ways are likely to bring those distortions with them; this shapes how they understand their clients, what they pathologize, and what they leave unexamined. If the field wants to maintain the trust of an ideologically diverse public, it might start by holding its own training programs to the same evidentiary standards it demands of its treatments.

item.title: Why Is It So Hard for Some People to Click "Like"?
item.description:
Social Comparison Theory

Why Is It So Hard for Some People to Click "Like"?

A missing "like" may reveal more about psychology than social media.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • A missing "like" can sometimes reflect psychological discomfort, not indifference.
  • Success can trigger social comparison and challenge how people see themselves.
  • Repeated silence may reveal relationship patterns more than isolated interactions.

Imagine this. You share something you've worked towards for years: a promotion, a degree, a published book, or a new business. Within minutes, people you barely know congratulate you. Strangers celebrate your success. Yet some of the people who know you best, the ones who watched your journey, heard your struggles, and witnessed your sacrifices, say nothing.

No "Congratulations."

No "Well done."

Not even a simple click on the "Like" button.

For many people, this silence feels surprisingly painful. After all, pressing "like" takes less than a second. It costs nothing. Why, then, can such a small action seem so difficult for some people?

The answer is that a "like" is rarely just a "like." Psychologically, it can represent recognition, acknowledgment, and acceptance. Sometimes, celebrating another person's success means confronting emotions we would rather avoid.

One explanation comes from social comparison theory, which suggests that people naturally evaluate themselves by comparing themselves with others. Most of us do this without even realising it. When someone else's achievement reflects something we also wanted, but have not yet attained, it can evoke feelings of inadequacy, disappointment, or envy. Your success may unintentionally become a reminder of someone else's unfinished dream.

Sometimes, however, the silence has less to do with comparison and more to do with consistency.

If someone has spent years doubting you, underestimating you, dismissing your ambitions, or subtly mocking your goals, your success creates a psychological problem. It challenges the story they have been telling themselves, and perhaps others, about who you are.

Psychologists refer to this as cognitive dissonance: the discomfort that arises when reality contradicts our beliefs. Imagine someone who confidently predicted that you would never finish your degree, never publish the book, or never build the career you envisioned. If you succeed, they have two choices. They can accept that they were wrong, or they can minimise, ignore, or avoid your achievement. For some people, silence feels easier than admitting they misjudged you.

This may also explain why some individuals who once criticised or even bullied others struggle to celebrate their accomplishments later. Bullying often depends on creating an imbalance of power. It places one person in the role of being "less capable," "less intelligent," or "less likely to succeed." When the person they underestimated succeeds, that imbalance disappears. Publicly congratulating them may feel, consciously or unconsciously, like acknowledging that their previous judgments no longer hold. For someone whose self-image depends on always being right or superior, that can be psychologically uncomfortable.

Recognition also has a social function. A public "Congratulations" is visible to everyone. It tells the world, I recognise this person's achievement. If someone has previously questioned your ability or encouraged others to doubt you, offering public praise may expose an inconsistency. Remaining silent allows them to avoid confronting both their own previous behaviour and the opinions of others.

Another explanation lies in how people experience success itself. Individuals with a scarcity mindset often see achievement as limited, almost as if success were a pie with only so many slices. Another person's accomplishment feels like one less opportunity for themselves. In contrast, people with an abundance mindset tend to experience someone else's success as inspiring rather than threatening. They understand that another person's promotion does not reduce their own potential, just as another author's book does not prevent them from writing their own.

Of course, not every missing "like" should be interpreted as hidden resentment. Some people rarely engage on social media. Others prefer private conversations over public comments. Some simply miss the post altogether. Human behaviour is far too complex to draw firm conclusions from a single online interaction.

What deserves more attention is not a single moment of silence but a consistent pattern. Does someone repeatedly disappear whenever you share good news? Do they celebrate everyone else's achievements while overlooking yours? Do they engage when you experience setbacks but remain absent when you thrive? Are they active online, yet somehow they always seem to miss your milestones? Have they discouraged you from pursuing ambitious goals, such as publishing a book, starting a business, or applying for a promotion, by offering unsolicited advice that emphasises the risks rather than the possibilities? On their own, these behaviours prove very little. Together, however, they may reveal something meaningful about the dynamics of the relationship. Patterns often speak louder than isolated incidents.

Perhaps the most psychologically secure people are those who celebrate others without hesitation. They understand that another person's success is not a verdict on their own worth. They can admire without comparing, encourage without competing, and congratulate without feeling diminished. Their self-esteem does not depend on being ahead of everyone else.

Perhaps the next time you share an achievement, don't rush to count the number of likes. Instead, notice the patterns. Who consistently celebrates your successes? Who quietly disappears whenever you accomplish something meaningful? Silence alone does not prove jealousy, resentment, or insecurity, but repeated silence in the face of your growth may tell you something about the relationship. The people who genuinely value you rarely feel diminished by your success; they celebrate it because your achievements do not threaten their sense of self. Sometimes, those who struggle most to acknowledge your success are not reacting to your achievement itself; they are reacting to what your achievement makes them feel about themselves.

item.title: The Hardest Part Isn't the Crisis
item.description:
Depression

The Hardest Part Isn't the Crisis

What the discharge sheet doesn't give you.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Most people leave the ER post mental health crisis with no real guidance on what comes next.
  • The gap between clinical knowledge and actual recovery is wider than most people expect.
  • Get one contact who knows what happened and can be reached if things worsen before a first appointment.

There is no real guide for when you leave the emergency room after a mental health crisis. I spent over two decades on the other side of that discharge desk. There is a reason you don't get a discharge guide; it is because we didn't have one to give you.

Our discharge instructions are often a few sheets of paper with some phone numbers to call for follow-up. There may be a prescription to fill at the pharmacy. The recommendation for the follow-up appointment is now for you to make.

What the ER Is Built For

The ER is very good at treating acute problems and crises. That is the part doctors train for obsessively. We stabilize patients but do not have a protocol for what happens after. You are released, and you're on your own. This is when recovery actually begins. It is the next 24 hours, the first 2 weeks, and the following months that matter. This is when the path becomes unclear for the patients, families, and loved ones.

I watched this happen to my patients, their families, and supporting friends. Patients were sent home into the same environment that played a role in causing the crisis. I told myself the referrals would work out, and people would follow up. I had to keep moving to the next patient.

I Became a Patient

My depression didn't start with lights and sirens; there wasn't an admitting crisis. It was slower than that, like a constant fade of my emotions, happiness, and myself. I was able to easily rationalize away these losses because I was still showing up to work, still functioning, and still making decisions under pressure. I knew all the signs of clinical depression and could have diagnosed it in anyone else in a few minutes. Yet I ignored them all in myself until I couldn't anymore.

I was sitting in a hospital parking lot after a long shift and just couldn't make myself start the car. Not because something dramatic had happened. I just was exhausted and had no energy left to continue this way. The weight of going home and pretending to be present was now more than I had left in me.

That's when I understood what my patients had been trying to tell me for years. I learned that knowing what's wrong and being able to do something about it are not the same thing. The distance between those two things is where people fall and need help.

The First 48 Hours

This is when recovery begins
Source: AI/ chatgpt image

If you are the patient or the person who is caring for someone, it is important to get one name and one direct phone number specifically for this next 48-hour timeframe. You need a specific person who knows what happened and who you can reach if things get worse before the first appointment. This could be a family member who's been briefed, a primary care nurse line, or somebody with this context.

Your discharge sheet covers the basics. You need a contact for this specific situation when urgent cares are closed, family physician offices are not open, or call lines only offer automation.

There is much more to discuss regarding the gap between stabilization and recovery.

What was the hardest part of that first week that no one prepared you for?

item.title: Parent and Adult Child Emotional Cage Fights
item.description:
Family Dynamics

Parent and Adult Child Emotional Cage Fights

Nine ways to make peace or move on after parent-adult child disputes.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional cage fights mean dumping vitriol, words that can't be unheard, onto another.
  • Let go of assumptions that the visceral shock of your words will inspire change in the other.
  • Take a deep breath and stay silent until you calm down a little or give each other time to cool off.
Source: AI-Generated

Reading about the recent cage fights on the South Lawn of the White House, I was reminded of the emotional violence that can happen between parents and adult children when pain begets pain and relationships are changed forever.

Jenna, whose beloved father committed suicide when she was 12 years old, has carried grief and fury all these years. Her fury is aimed at her mother, who scrambled to get a job to support the family after her husband's death. Since then, Jenna has picked fights with her mother over things both minor and major. Her animosity culminated in a screaming match recently as she blamed her mother for all the difficulties of her life, both past and present, and finished her tirade off with, “And you’re the reason Daddy killed himself!”

“That took my breath away,” Jenna’s mother Amy told me recently. “My husband was bipolar and refused to take his medications. It was hard living with him and even harder to lose him in that way. I did the best I could at the time. Her words hurt me deeply. I'm her mother. I'll love her forever. But I don't know if I can ever like or trust her again."

Examples of Emotional Cage Fights in Families

I’ve seen a variety of emotional cage fights in therapy sessions. These are situations where one or both people express unfiltered rage, saying words that can't be unsaid or unheard.

There was the father who screamed at his accomplished, professionally successful daughter that she was “the worst disappointment of my life, a real loser…” because she was no longer attending Catholic Sunday Mass and, instead, was going to an Episcopalian church with an activist female pastor whom she liked and admired.

There was the mother who so disapproved of her 30-year-old son living with his girlfriend that she told him in a cold variation of cage fighting that he was no longer her son and that she never wanted to see him again.

There was the boy in his late teens who, during a therapy session, yelled something at his mother that was so lewd and profane that it's unprintable. And his mother answered him with similar vitriol. Any reasonable resolution of their issues suddenly seemed impossible as rage and deep resentment hung in the air.

There are many instances where a parent or an adult child may be righteously angry. There may be unresolved trauma from the past. Or a growing conviction that having a relationship with the other person is neither possible nor desirable.

How to Avoid Verbal Battles and Reduce Rancor

What can you do to resolve differences or go your separate ways without resorting to verbal battles that leave nothing but pain and continuing rancor between you?

  1. Let go of the assumption that your parent or adult child will change because you demand it or because of the visceral shock of your words. You can't change another person. You can only change yourself—or how you react to a particular situation with your parent or your adult child. Dumping vitriol on the other can indeed be a shock, but it doesn't do anything to inspire positive change or compassionate compromises.
  2. Realize that bringing up the past repeatedly and resentfully solves nothing. Think about it. You can't go back and change the past. Being reminded of all the mistakes you made as a parent or the horror of your rebellious adolescence does nothing to inspire growth beyond a painful past. Focus on the present and what might be possible now. Notice the ways you both may have grown and changed since the bad old days.
  3. Know that emotional cage fighting can lead to an estrangement that neither of you may want. When you spew venom that can't be unsaid or unheard, it can build emotional barriers anew. When someone feels under attack, their defensiveness and your rage can block any meaningful communication.
  4. Inflicting pain is not productive. It can be a temptation to strike back at someone who has traumatized or hurt you deeply. But it is more productive to deal with your trauma and/or anger in therapy, discovering, over time, a way forward to a healthier, happier life.
  5. Realize that some things can’t be unsaid—or unheard. When a parent is blamed for her partner's suicide or when a parent vehemently rejects a child who is coming out, those words hang between parent and child in a way that can't be erased by later apologies.
  6. When you feel a rage attack coming on, breathe deeply and stay silent while you choose your words carefully. Taking time to sort through your feelings may preclude dumping vitriol on the other and escalating your conflict.
  7. Give each other a timeout. This can be particularly helpful if you're in a shouting match where communication has stopped and hurled insults are fueling your anger and causing you to tune each other out.
  8. Make the decision to forgive for yourself, not for the other person. Carrying the burden of anger and resentment over the past can weigh you down emotionally for years to come. Making the decision to forgive and let go isn't easy. But it may help to tell yourself that this isn't to let the other person off easily or to negate the pain of what happened between you in the past. It's a way to lighten your emotional load as you continue on with your life.
  9. Take responsibility for your own life. That’s the path to freedom. Some people are locked into anger, old and new, in unending conflict with a parent or an adult child.

The mother who demands closeness, building her life around busy adult children who don't desire frequent contact, is dooming herself to daily disappointment and feelings of rejection.

The adult child stuck in blaming mode with a parent over events that took place decades ago may have trouble building a new life beyond that pain.

Feeling stuck in a painful place can lead to some ugly moments that only increase the emotional chasm between you. Whether you are able to resolve your differences or decide to go your separate ways, taking the responsibility for your own growth and happiness from now on can enhance your life immeasurably.

item.title: "Love Island USA" Season 8 and Modern Dating’s Evolution on TV
item.description:
Media

"Love Island USA" Season 8 and Modern Dating’s Evolution on TV

Consistency, clarity, and communication still matter in dating.

Posted July 29, 2026

Key points
  • Modern dating has evolved, but the foundations of healthy relationships have not.
  • Too many options can make it harder to fully invest in a relationship.
  • Communication is about ensuring that your actions consistently match your words.
Source: Marlon Trottmann / Pexels

Every generation believes dating has become more complicated. And it’s possible that that's true.

When talking about dating today, people mention dating apps, situationships, soft launches, and an ever-growing list of relationship labels. Previous generations navigated different social expectations.

While the circumstances of how to date may change, the end goal is still the same: finding a relationship in which both people feel understood, respected, and emotionally secure.

Season 8 of “Love Island USA” became one of the most talked-about seasons because it reflected many of the conversations already happening outside the villa. Yes, reality television exaggerates conflict for entertainment. But beneath the dramatic recouplings, bombshells, and movie night reveals were relationship dynamics many people recognize from their own lives.

Modern dating may look different than it did a generation ago, but healthy relationships still depend on three things: consistency, clarity, and communication.

The grass isn’t always greener.

The part of “Love Island” that most people get excited about is the bombshells. Just as the original contestants are beginning to settle into one connection, another possibility walks into the villa.

While most people aren't dating in front of cameras, the experience isn’t entirely unfamiliar. Because of dating and social media, potential “new” possibilities are more prominent. This constant access can make it tempting to wonder whether someone even more compatible might be waiting just around the corner.

Psychologists have long described this as a “grass is greener” effect, which is the tendency to believe satisfaction exists somewhere else rather than in what we already have. Research has found that too many options can actually make decision-making more difficult and reduce satisfaction with the choices we make because we tend to focus on what we might be missing rather than what we're building.

Season 8 continuously displayed this phenomenon. Contestants often struggle to decide whether to continue investing in an existing relationship or pursue the excitement of someone new. The challenge wasn’t having to choose between two (or more) people. The challenge is really deciding whether the person should stop searching and start investing.

Healthy relationships don't require settling, but they do require giving a connection enough time and attention to discover what it could become.

Labels aren't always useful.

Other than the grass appearing greener, many people talked about the labels. Viewers constantly debated whether certain islanders were truly exclusive, or caught somewhere in the increasingly familiar territory of a situationship.

Labels allow people to communicate expectations and understand where a relationship stands.

While labels can be helpful to create a shared language, they’re only useful if everyone defines them the same way.

For one person, a situationship may mean exclusive emotional commitment without an unofficial title. For someone else, it may simply describe getting to know multiple people without the expectation of exclusivity. Even the word relationship varies from person to person.

Many psychologists believe that even consistent communication can produce misunderstandings. And it’s not because they’re not talking, but because they’re either talking at the wrong time or not talking about the harder stuff.

Shared words don't always mean shared understanding.

Season 8 captured this dynamic repeatedly. Many disagreements weren't necessarily about commitment itself; they were about two people operating from different assumptions without realizing it. Knowing where you stand matters more than finding the perfect label.

Communication is more than talking.

Gen Z is often described as the most emotionally open generation. There have been more conversations about emotional security and mental health now than compared to previous generations.

This is great because it's a positive shift toward openness and a willingness to hear others out.

But communication isn't measured by how often we talk about our feelings. It's measured by whether our words and behaviors consistently tell the same story.

One of the season’s most talked-about examples involves Sincere, who was quickly nicknamed “inSincere” on TikTok after reassuring Melanie about the connection while behaving very differently when she wasn't around.

Viewers weren't just reacting because he explored another connection. That possibility is built into the format of the show. They reacted because his words and actions appeared to be telling different stories.

This disconnect between what someone says and what they do is the biggest source of confusion in relationships. We naturally want to believe what people tell us, especially when it matches up with what we hope is true. But trust isn't built through reassurance alone. It's built through consistency.

Movie Night became such a defining moment this season for the same reason. Contestants finally saw the conversations and behaviors they hadn’t previously witnessed. For some, the footage confirmed what they had suspected all along. For others, it challenged the version of the relationship they believed they were building.

Outside the villa, relationships don’t come with a highlight reel of everything you missed. Instead, clarity develops over time as patterns pop up. Healthy communication is making sure your words match your actions. It's about creating enough consistency that another person doesn't have to wonder which version of you they're going to encounter.

Nothing is more certain than change.

Every generation dates differently. Technology changes. Social expectations progress. And new terms enter the conversation and old dating rules fade away.

Those changes are simply part of how relationships adapt over time. What doesn't change, however, is what people need to feel secure in a relationship. Perhaps that's why “Love Island USA” Season 8 resonated with so many viewers.

Consistency allows trust to grow. Clarity helps people understand where they stand. And most importantly, communication creates the foundation for both.
